components.text: The decisive demand contacted is whether ordinary moral commitment supports the realist, attitude-independent interpretation rather than merely defining it.
The cruelty verdict might be widely shared without ordinary speakers possessing a determinate metaethical commitment.
Whether familiar first-order reactions establish a widely held determinate realist commitment.
The contacted component is whether evidence about ordinary responses warrants attributing the attitude-independent metaethical position to respondents.
Responses to concrete normative cases may be mistaken for answers to distinct metaethical questions.
Whether ordinary responses to moral cases reliably reveal attitude-independent metaethical commitments.
The decisive component contacted is whether the asserted realist seeming is shared enough to support the metaethical conclusion beyond the person reporting it.
Private appearances do not by themselves publicly establish that attitude-independent facts exist.
Whether the cruelty judgment remains wrong independently of approval, belief, sentiment, or convention.
The decisive demand is the purported exhaustiveness of falsity, attitude-dependent truth, and non-propositionality as alternatives to objective moral facts.
Context-sensitive use may preserve proposition-like moral discourse without imposing one uniform semantic analysis.
Whether rejecting error theory, stance dependence, and non-cognitivism exhausts the alternatives and yields realism.
Whether propositional behavior forces one uniform realist semantic analysis across moral-language contexts.
The decisive demand is whether the intuitive cruelty verdict genuinely contradicts error theory rather than importing assumptions about the error theorist's attitudes and conduct.
The move distinguishes error theory's denial of objective facts from pragmatic implications about what its adherents approve or do.
Whether intuitive resistance to cruelty under changed attitudes directly counts against error theory.
The decisive demand is whether realism must itself be an explicit folk intuition to qualify as supported by common-sense moral judgment.
Difficulty understanding direct metaethical questions does not prevent reasoning from clearer first-order judgments.
Whether realism must itself be a directly grasped and widely held folk metaethical position.
Whether failure to elicit direct metaethical intuitions blocks a common-sense route to realism.
The decisive component contacted is whether contextual variation rules out identifiable contexts with genuinely realist moral content.
Determinate realist content may occur in specialized deliberative contexts even if ordinary speakers are often indeterminate.
The academic ethics example aims to distinguish assertion about wrongness from reports of attitudes or attempts at influence.
Whether contextual variability prevents any relevant moral assertion from having genuinely realist content.
The decisive demand contacted is whether meaningful moral assertion in a context must carry determinate realist or anti-realist semantic commitments.
Holistic communicative meaning can preserve meaningful embedded and assertoric use without a uniform metaethical analysis.
Meaningful first-order judgments need not settle the metaethical inference drawn from them.
Whether meaningful moral assertion requires determinate realist or anti-realist semantic commitments.
The decisive component contacted is whether English conceptual practice must correspond to one determinate underlying phenomenon or semantic structure.
Rejecting a fixed word-to-phenomenon correspondence leaves additional conceptual space outside the elimination argument.
First-order or ordinary conceptual use may not determine the metaphilosophical structure required by the realist inference.
Whether the realist elimination remains exhaustive once its linguistic and metaphilosophical assumptions are rejected.
The decisive demand contacted is whether philosophical and first-order intuitions are sufficiently pre-theoretical and representative to ground the realist inference.
Seemings elicited through philosophical framing may reflect learned response patterns rather than universal truth detection.
Specialized philosophical contexts may generate idiosyncratic judgments rather than uniquely reveal realist semantic content.
Whether the specific cruelty judgment is an attitude-independent intellectual appearance with evidential force.
The decisive component contacted is whether cultural or linguistic variation eliminates shared normative conceptual resources altogether.
Shared thin concepts may persist even where explicit metaethical commitments and thicker concepts vary.
Conceptual variation in terms such as knowledge need not generalize to all thin normative comparisons.
Whether cultural and linguistic variation undermines all shared normative concepts or intuitions.
Whether conceptual variation eliminates cross-context normative continuity altogether.
The contacted practical component is whether shared normative vocabulary carries stance-independent importance or authority for an agent.
Even if stance-independent facts existed, their motivational importance would not follow independently of an agent's goals.
Whether at least some moral truths remain valid independently of attitudes.
The decisive component contacted is whether objective morality claims a kind of authority that cannot be escaped merely by citing contrary preferences.
Whether objective moral reasons possess authority that cannot be reduced to an agent's preferences.
The decisive component contacted is whether preference-based motivation can sustain costly moral conduct when stronger self-directed preference satisfaction is available.
The claim that objectivity affects commitment is behavioral rather than an answer to the training-based epistemic challenge.
Whether preference-based practical importance can sustain costly moral commitment as strongly as objective moral reasons.
The decisive demand contacted is whether accepting anti-realism predictably weakens moral conduct rather than having contingent empirical effects.
Realism's alleged authority does not entail beneficial conduct and might coexist with dogmatism or rationalized harm.
Whether anti-realism itself implies weaker moral behavior or reduced costly beneficence.
Whether realism itself reliably supplies beneficial motivational or behavioral authority.
The decisive component contacted is what an intuition is and whether it is merely an asserted belief produced by philosophical inference or training.
The definition permits different subjects to have different appearances and does not treat an intuition as publicly compulsory proof.
The epistemic definition does not address the later empirical dispute about behavior.
Whether ethical intuitions should be treated as trained reports or as a recognizable class of intellectual appearances.
What kind of mental state an ethical intuition is before questions of shared public justification arise.
The decisive component contacted is whether a subject's intellectual appearance can supply initial justification even without public corroboration.
The argument supplies a general presumption for appearances but does not specifically defeat the proposed training-based defeater.
The general epistemic argument does not establish that the content of every concept or word is determinate.
Whether the private character of an appearance deprives it of prima facie justificatory standing for the subject.
Whether possible distortion warrants rejecting any initial presumption in favor of appearances.
